series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/4] block: do not issue background swap bios as root
series_items.patch_summary: This RFC patch proposes to modify the behavior of bio_issue_as_root_blkg() to not issue background swap bios as root, allowing cgroup IO controllers to throttle such I/O operations. The change is motivated by the need to prevent memory deadlocks in certain scenarios, specifically when using dm-crypt and dm-thin with limit_swap_bios.

review_comments.author: Christoph Hellwig
review_comments.summary: Identified a potential issue with REQ_BACKGROUND marking I/O as not urgent, which could lead to throttling and foreground paging. Suggested reevaluating the patch's design in light of this concern.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon, Sep 28, 2026 at 10:18:36AM +0200, Alexandre Ghiti wrote:
> bio_issue_as_root_blkg() issues every REQ_SWAP bio as root, bypassing
> the cgroup IO controllers, because reclaim cannot stall indefinitely on
> swap writes. Some swap writes are not urgent though: zswap writeback is
> best effort.
> 
> Such a bio cannot simply drop REQ_SWAP: dm-crypt and dm-thin rely on it
> for limit_swap_bios, which caps in-flight swap bios to avoid a memory
> deadlock, see commit a666e5c05e7c ("dm: fix deadlock when swapping to
> encrypted device").

Is that true?  REQ_BACKGROUND very much implies the I/O can the throttled
and thus better not be foreground paging, and thus the caller should be
able to tolerate a failure.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 2/4] mm/zswap: turn shrink_memcg_cb()'s argument into a flags word
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the `shrink_memcg_cb()` function in the zswap module to accept a flags word instead of a boolean pointer as an argument. The flags word allows callers to pass additional information, specifically whether the walk stopped at an entry already in the swap cache. This change does not introduce any functional changes but rather provides a more flexible way for callers to interact with the function. The patch defines a new flag `ZSWAP_SHRINK_SWAPCACHE` and updates the function's logic accordingly.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 3/4] mm/zswap: allow writeback to be throttled by the cgroup IO controllers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows the cgroup IO controllers to throttle zswap writeback operations by introducing a new 'throttled' flag in the swap_io_ctx structure. When this flag is set, the write operation is issued as background I/O instead of being exempt from cgroup throttling, which avoids priority inversion and ensures that memory reclaim is not stalled for other workloads.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 4/4] mm/zswap: move reclaim-driven writeback to a kworker
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the reclaim-driven writeback of zswap to a kworker, which writes back data in chunks of SWAP_CLUSTER_MAX entries at a time while holding a reference on the memcg. This change is made to prevent stalls caused by uninterruptible sleeps when the owning cgroup's IO budget is exceeded. The shrinker now reports nothing freed until the worker has run and completed the writeback.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary:

review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the deferred writeback workers hold a reference to the memcg, and requested that queued workers be stopped before calling try_to_unmap() to prevent lock ordering violations.

Reviewer noted that the current implementation may not scale as the number of workers increases, requesting further testing and discussion.

Reviewer Alexandre Ghiti noted that the writeback bio is issued as root, incurring debt to the cgroup, and with this series throttling the bio at submission, reclaimers would stall on a single cgroup's IO budget; he suggested deferring writeback for everyone.

review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Nhat,

On Tue, Sep 29, 2026 at 3:43 PM Nhat Pham <nphamcs@gmail.com> wrote:

---

It would not scale indeed, the worker does not accumulate in this
version of the patch. That needs to be tested and discussed.

---

Today the writeback bio is issued as root, which incurs debt to the
cgroup. The submitting task repays it on return to user or on any
other IO of the cgroup until the debt is paid off.

With this series the bio is throttled at submission instead, so
whoever submits it sleeps until the cgroup has budget:
- for direct reclaimers, that's the application latency we observed
- for kswapd reclaim, it would stall on a single cgroup's IO budget

So we need to defer for everyone.

---

In the large production workload I have worked on, when the shrinker
is enabled, the zswap pool size decreases by ~97%. So I did not want
to accumulate "too much" work to prevent zswap from draining "hot"
pages, it acts like an additional throttling mechanism. But that needs
discussion, hence the RFC.

And you're right, In the next version, I'll clearly point out all the
behavioral changes I made with their justifications.

---

Yes, this is another behavioural change that I will explain in the next version.

Indeed the work piles up in the shrinker control loop if writeback
cannot catch up but note that it is bounded, which is what we want
right?

---

You're right, and the explanation is "we cannot starve other memcgs if
one worker stalls because it exhausted its memcg budget".

Thanks Nhat!

Alex

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the performance of zswap shrinker on systems running iocost by addressing two issues: (1) zswap writeback is issued as root and charged to the cgroup afterwards, causing stalls in application allocations; and (2) throttled writes sleep in their submitter, often an application thread. The patches modify zswap to mark writebacks as REQ_BACKGROUND instead of REQ_SWAP, allowing them to be throttled by iocost controllers. Additionally, patch 4 moves reclaim-driven writeback to a per-lruvec kworker, reducing the impact on application threads. The series includes benchmarks showing significant performance improvements for various workloads.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 1/7] mm: support promotion-only NUMA hinting scans
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new mode for NUMA hinting scans that only promotes pages to higher tiers without scanning the entire VMA. The global balancing mode is used to determine the intent of an individual protection walk, and the patch adds a new flag MM_CP_PROT_NUMA_PROMO_ONLY to select this promotion-only mode. The change-protection flags are built in task_numa_work() based on the balancing mode, and folio_can_map_prot_numa() derives the single-threaded private state at the point of use instead of adding another precomputed boolean to the protection-walk interface. This patch is required for memory-tiering fixes and must be accompanied by them when backported.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 2/7] mm: allow shared folios to be promoted to a fast tier
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows shared copy-on-write folios and executable file folios mapped by multiple processes to be promoted from slow memory to a faster tier, as long as the migration is from south to north. This change enables promotion for low-tier folios to top-tier, but maintains existing restrictions for ordinary placement and non-promotion migrations. The patch also renames the `folio_use_access_time` function to `folio_numab_promotable` to better reflect its purpose.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 3/7] sched/numa: scan read-only file mappings in tiering mode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the NUMA balancing code to scan read-only file mappings when tiering is enabled, but only performs promotion scans on these mappings. This change allows hot file folios on slow memory to be promoted to faster memory, preventing them from getting stuck in slower memory. The patch also retains the existing restriction of excluding shared libraries from migration. With this change, binary tier residency can track runtime hotness more accurately.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 4/7] sched/numa: separate VMA placement from scan continuation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the logic of VMA placement from scan continuation in the Linux kernel's scheduling and NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) code. The existing `vma_is_accessed` function returned true for both placement eligibility and scan progress, which made it difficult to distinguish between these two states. The patch introduces a new function `vma_needs_placement_scan` that handles placement eligibility, while the `task_numa_work` function is modified to handle scan continuation state. This separation allows PID-inactive VMAs to be scanned for promotion without treating scan continuation as evidence of placement eligibility, which is a prerequisite for a subsequent fix.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 5/7] sched/numa: scan PID-inactive VMAs for promotion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) memory management to bypass a filter that suppresses faults needed to promote hot slow-tier memory. The filter, which skips VMAs without recent PID activity, is disabled for promotion-only scans and only enabled when a VMA scan starts. This change allows for more efficient scanning of large VMAs and reduces the risk of starving in-progress placement scans. The patch also introduces a new field to track the last completed placement scan separately from other scans. With this modification, memory tiering can adapt to changing workloads and improve system performance.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 6/7] mm: use BIT() for change_protection() flags
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the MM_CP_* flags in include/linux/mm.h to use the BIT() macro consistently, replacing open-coded shifts. This change does not introduce any functional changes and is intended to improve code readability and maintainability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 7/7] mm: use VMA flag helpers in NUMA balancing
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the NUMA balancing code in the Linux kernel to use VMA flag helpers instead of directly accessing vm_flags. This change is made to improve code readability and maintainability by encapsulating the logic for checking specific flags within the VMA structure. The existing flag predicates remain unchanged, and no functional changes are intended. The patch applies to three files: kernel/sched/fair.c, mm/internal.h, and mm/migrate.c.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses poor NUMA balancing behavior in a production deployment by stopping VMA scan filters from gating memory-tier promotion. The issue arises because the global balancing mode cannot describe the intent of an individual VMA/PTE walk (placement vs promotion). To fix this, the patch plumbs scan reasoning into the prot_none injection while retaining placement-scan filtering. It introduces promotion-only NUMA protection walks and derives private VMA state in the folio eligibility check. The patches also separate VMA placement eligibility from partial-scan continuation and scan PID-inactive VMAs for promotion. Additionally, it uses BIT() for change_protection flags and the VMA flag API in touched NUMA-balancing code.

review_comments.raw_body:
On 30 Sep 2026, at 10:50, Gregory Price wrote:

> On Wed, Sep 30, 2026 at 10:02:23PM +0800, Li Zhe wrote:
>> The use case is closer to the second one, but the main motivation is not
>> only startup-time performance. The more important point is that each
>> workload has its own DDR/CXL budget assigned by the workload manager.
>>
>
> mempolicy is the wrong interface to do budget policy, you'd be better
> off looking at Joshua's memcg tiered node solutions for that.
>
>> MPOL_WEIGHTED_INTERLEAVE is useful because it lets new allocations
>> follow that per-workload budget from the beginning, instead of placing
>> everything on one tier first and correcting the placement later. This is
>> important for workload orchestration because the workload starts from a
>> placement close to its assigned DDR/CXL ratio.
>>
>
> This however is reasonable to me - you'd prefer to spread out the cost
> of initial faulting placement explicitly, rather than simply take
> fallbacks when the top-tier budget becomes pressured.
>
> i.e. w/o interleave:
>
> [node 0       ]
> ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ alloc until full
>                 vvvvvvvvv fallback
>                 [node 1          ]
>
> in this scenario you end up with considerable hot memory
> on the remote node consolidated in time-space (everything
> allocated after node0 becomes full skews heavily toward
> node1)
>
> Tiering then likely takes many faults to rebalance after
> you've already reached node0 limits.
>
> w/ interleave
>
> [node 0                                      ]
>  ^^^vv^^^vv^^^vv^^^vv^^^vv^^^vv....
> [node 1                                      ]
>
> In this scenario you do an initial fill distributed by weight
> and then let tiering figure it out without consolidating all
> of the pressure to the point where node0 has no space left.
>
> That said - this seems like mostly an initial-fill problem, after
> you initially fill your memory, a new allocation largely implies
> the memory is hot - and you probably prefer that to be local.

If this is a initial-fill problem, can userspace set weighted interleave
initially? The program or harness can observe memory usage of the program
or related NUMA nodes and switch the policy to numa balancing via
set_mempolicy() or mbind() without MPOL_MF_MOVE after certain threshold
is met?



Best Regards,
Yan, Zi

patches_reviewed.patch_summary: Patch aims to clamp negative cpu_clock() skew, but reviewers raise concerns about the implementation and its impact on x86 architecture.

review_comments.author: David Stevens
review_comments.summary: Identified a potential issue with rdtsc() producing non-monotonic results on x86, which could explain the negative skew. Suggested adding a rbm() to match the behavior of rdtsc_ordered().
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Sep 30, 2026 at 8:19 AM Peter Zijlstra <peterz@infradead.org> wrote:
>
> On Wed, Sep 30, 2026 at 10:22:52AM -0400, Johannes Weiner wrote:
> > On Tue, Sep 29, 2026 at 10:17:40AM +0200, Peter Zijlstra wrote:
> > > On Tue, Sep 29, 2026 at 10:10:04AM +0200, Peter Zijlstra wrote:
> > >
> > > > > When running browser workloads on an Intel N100 with a sustained
> > > > > psi.mem.some of 2-3%, this underflow is observed once every couple of
> > > > > hours.
> > >
> > > Reading is hard. This is sad, that's a relatively modern chip :-(
> >
> > I'm still struggling, but I'm under the weather so bear with me.
> >
> > That's a cpu_clock() implementation issue, right? "The value for
> > cpu_clock(i) is monotonic for constant i". Presumably violating that
> > would be a problem beyond psi?
>
> Yeah, although most everybody has a filter on top for some reason or
> another.
>
> Mostly it could happen that when the watchdog would detect the TSC
> wasn't stable after all, you'd be up a creek if you didn't also have
> this filter.
>
> But I'm very sad to see modern chips have shit TSC, that wasn't supposed
> to happen.

I ran artificial memory pressure tests on the other two devices I have
at hand - one with an Intel i5-1245U and one with an Intel Ultra 5
325. Both devices also observed negative elapsed durations. The
artificial workloads were much heavier and actually produced negative
elapsed durations every couple of minutes. So this doesn't look like a
platform-specific issue.

For reference, the negative elapsed durations I saw averaged a little
under 100ns. The largest duration I saw was 371ns.

If I'm following the code correctly, cpu_clock() on x86 ends up
calling rdtsc() via sched_clock(). The rdtsc() function is documented
to produce non-monotonic results when compared across CPUs, since the
rdtsc instruction can read the tsc out of order relative to other
instructions. If that results in get_recent_times() reading the tsc
before it reads the psi state, then I think that would explain the
negative skew. I added a rbm() immediately before the call to
cpu_clock() in get_recent_times() to match the behavior of
rdtsc_ordered(), and with that I didn't see any negative elapsed
durations during overnight testing. This does suggest that calling
through to sched_clock() might not provide strong enough guarantees on
x86 to satisfy the cpu_clock() contract.

-David

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm: page_alloc: make defrag_mode retries follow the promoted order

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the behavior of page allocation in defrag_mode to make retries follow the promoted order, rather than the original request order. This change is intended to prevent indefinite retrying by requests that are not movable, which can lead to reclaim storms and excessive memory pressure. The patch treats promoted requests as costly orders, resetting progress counters for them and checking compaction results at the promoted order. It also resets retry counters when a fallback attempt is taken, allowing it to get a full retry budget before the OOM killer is considered. This change aims to improve performance and reduce memory pressure in systems with high inode churn under memory.low protection.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses two issues in the cgroup struct_ops query mechanism. First, it introduces a new function `cgroup_bpf_enabled_runtime()` to handle dynamic attach type selection, which resolves an issue with constant evaluation by the compiler when multiple attach types are present. series_items.patch_summary: This RFC patch proposes a fix for the struct_ops attach infrastructure in the Linux kernel's bpf and cgroup subsystems. The problem it addresses is that the current implementation assumes there will only be one struct_ops attach type, but this assumption breaks when a second attach type is added. To solve this issue, the patch introduces a new function, cgroup_bpf_enabled_runtime(), which reads the key instead of relying on static_branch_unlikely(). Additionally, the patch modifies find_atype_by_struct_ops_id() to skip slots with type_id 0, ensuring that queries for non-existent attach types return -ENOENT.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 2/4] memcg_ext: add cgroup-attached bpf_memcg_ops
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds an empty bpf_memcg_ops type to allow attaching memory policies to cgroups, which is the first step in making memcg enforcement programmable one hook at a time. The patch also moves cgroup BPF attach types outside of CONFIG_CGROUP_BPF and fixes struct_ops registration stubs for all supported configurations. This does not change any existing behavior yet.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 3/4] memcg_ext: allow BPF to defer memory.high enforcement
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) programs to defer memory.high enforcement, which prevents tasks holding kernel locks from being stuck in the charge path. It introduces high_policy ops that provide a read-only snapshot of the charge and allow programs to return a request. This approach enables more efficient handling of memory allocation and deallocation by allowing BPF programs to skip inline calls and re-entering the charge path.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 4/4] selftests/bpf: add a cgroupfs lock-holder bpf_memcg_ops sample
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) sample to track and enforce policies on tasks holding cgroupfs kernfs locks. The policy, called bpf_memcg_ops, prevents tasks from being inline memory.high enforced if they hold such locks. It does this by tracking the depth of kernfs_rwsem and kernfs_supers_rwsem locks per task using fentry/fexit hooks. Two counters are used to guard against incorrect enforcement. The patch is measured to improve performance on a reproducer, reducing stall times and increasing throughput.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series, memcg_ext, introduces a new struct_ops type called bpf_memcg_ops to attach memory controller policy to a cgroup through a cgroup-attached struct_ops. The goal is to prevent tasks from being stuck while holding kernel locks due to memory reclaim and throttling. A specific problem addressed by this patch is the kernfs notify worker, which can be stuck while holding the cgroup2 kernfs_rwsem lock. The patch adds a new policy called high_policy that allows policies to specify where memory.high should be enforced instead of inlining the call. Measurements show significant improvements in performance and latency compared to the baseline and an existing fix for a similar problem.

review_comments.author: Yafang Shao
review_comments.summary: Reviewer suggested that the policy should notify userspace via ringbuf when it defers debt, and proposed a userspace reclaimer to handle the reclaim through memory.reclaim; they also proposed using clone3(CLONE_INTO_CGROUP) to charge CPU usage of the spawned reclaimer to the target cgroup
review_comments.raw_body:
Hello Shakeel,

On the open question of how deferred debt eventually gets paid: would
it make sense for the policy to also notify userspace (e.g. via
ringbuf) when it defers, and have a userspace reclaimer do the reclaim
through memory.reclaim?

I understand one of the concerns for the async worker is CPU
accounting. If the concern is that the kworker's CPU usage is not
charged to the target cgroup, the userspace reclaimer could instead be
spawned with clone3(CLONE_INTO_CGROUP) so it runs inside the target
cgroup, and both its CPU and memory usage get charged there.

One caveat: intermediate cgroups with the no-internal-process
constraint cannot take processes, so this would only work for leaf
cgroups.

What do you think?

An LLM helped me quickly implement a userspace async memcg reclaimer
based on your series, and it seems to work quite well.

Sure. On our production servers we have been running a set of BPF
programs to tailor kernel behavior for different workloads — all of
them global programs so far — and I believe they are all good
candidates for per-cgroup BPF policies now that cgroup-attached
struct_ops is available. They have been really helpful in our
Kubernetes production environment. I have sent some of them upstream,
such as:

  - BPF-THP
    https://lwn.net/Articles/1039689/
  - BPF-auto-NUMA
    https://lwn.net/Articles/1054030/

Perhaps we can revisit both of them and turn them into per-cgroup
policies — what do you think?

We are also running some custom BPF programs that have not been sent
upstream yet, such as:

  - BPF-async-reclaimer
    We don't care about the CPU accounting of the kworker, so we just
wake up a kworker to do the async reclaiming.
  - BPF-fault-around

We are planning a few more customizations to resolve painful
production issues, such as:

  - The long-standing inode::lock contention caused by dentries [0].
    We have not started implementing it yet, but we might introduce a
memcg->dentry_limit or a memcg->vfs_cache_pressure as BPF policies..

rest are per-cgroup MM policies that would need the
struct_ops-to-cgroup mechanism generalized beyond memcg — which is why
I hope these use cases can help make the design more generic.

[0] https://lore.kernel.org/linux-fsdevel/20240511200240.6354-2-torvalds@linux-foundation.org/

-- 
Regards
Yafang

review_comments.author: Shakeel Butt (author)
review_comments.summary:
The author acknowledges that the default behavior for memory.high should be changed and is open to increasing the threshold from MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH to a larger number, but wants to keep this decision separate from the initial proposal. They also plan to provide a mechanism for users to specify custom behavior and introduce async reclaim workers.

Author acknowledged that kthreads need to schedule high_work like tasks do, agreed to extend best-effort reclaim to kthreads, but still needs to examine userspace tasks.
review_comments.raw_body:
Please correct me if I misunderstood you. Mainly, you are saying that we
should have a sane default behavior for memory.high. At the moment, if the
current charging process accumulates charges totaling more than
MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH pages and the target memcg is over its high limit,
memory.high is enforced synchronously. You are suggesting that we should
increase the threshold from MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH to some arbitrarily large
number. In that case, synchronous enforcement of memory.high will be very
rare.

I am fine with changing the default behavior. Actually, I have been
contemplating whether I should propose a revert of commit c9afe31ec443e
("memcg: synchronously enforce memory.high for large overcharges") because
it has introduced more problems than it has solved, but that is a separate
topic. The initial commit already mentioned that MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH was used
arbitrarily, so replacing it with something big might be acceptable. I want
to keep that decision separate.

I am not sure about annotating specific paths. I think it would impose a
greater maintenance burden as the kernel evolves, since the annotations
might become stale. Also, people might object to adding memcg-internal hooks
in non-memcg code paths. In any case, this can be explored separately.

Returning to the actual proposal, my plan was to start small with a narrow,
specific use case. However, my long-term plan is to provide a mechanism to
change the default behavior for custom use cases. For example, for
memory.high, I will provide a way for users to specify what behavior they
want, i.e., whether or not they want more synchronous throttling. Second, I
will introduce a mechanism to trigger async reclaim workers. I also plan to
extend this functionality to memory.max. I just wanted to convey that I will
keep pushing this proposal, with the use cases adjusted a bit.

---

Yes, that makes sense. When a non-task-context charge exceeds memory.high,
the kernel already schedules high_work for the charged memcg. I plan to do
the same for kthreads so they need not reclaim or throttle inline. This is
best-effort reclaim rather than exact debt accounting; I still need to
examine userspace tasks that charge another memcg through
set_active_memcg(). I am addressing the reclaim worker's CPU accounting
separately.

Thanks for taking a look and providing feedback.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] scsi: mpi3mr: Poll a reply queue that an interrupt found busy
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a situation where an interrupt handler for the MPI3MR SCSI device returns without processing a reply queue, leaving it busy and unprocessed until the next interrupt or command timeout. To fix this, the patch sets a flag to enable polling of the reply queue when it is found busy, allowing the IRQ thread to process any pending replies.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/2] scsi: mpi3mr: Stop IRQ polling when no reply is ready
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the MPI3MR SCSI driver to stop IRQ polling when no reply is ready on a queue, reducing CPU usage and improving performance. The driver previously polled queues for about 45 seconds, waking every ~20us, which was inefficient. The change introduces an empty check while owning the queue, allowing the driver to switch back to interrupts once a poll finds the queue empty. This approach reduces the number of wakeups from 236 times per I/O to twice per I/O, resulting in significant CPU savings and improved throughput for certain workloads.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a performance issue in the mpi3mr driver, where IRQ polling is performed excessively when there are many pending I/Os. The patch introduces a mechanism to stop IRQ polling when no reply is ready, reducing CPU usage and improving system responsiveness. This is achieved by modifying the driver's behavior when an interrupt finds a busy reply queue, allowing it to hand over ownership of the queue to a thread instead of continuing to poll.
